11163-potterism-a-tragi-farcical-tract:
Rose Macaulay published this 1920 tragi-farcical tract, dedicated to the unsentimental precisians in thought, who have no fit habitation on this confused, inaccurate, and emotional planet. Epigraphs from Johnson, Bacon, Gilbert, and Evelyn Underhill attack cant, loose talk, and the egocentric habit of asking what use a thing is to me.

The novel is told in four parts, by R. M. , by Gideon, by Lelia Yorke, and by Katherine Varick. Parts cover potters and anti-potters, opportunity, Jane and Clare, spinning, dining with the Hobarts, seeing Jane, the terrible tragedy on the stairs, and an awful suspicion. Lelia wonders whether Jane knew or only suspected her husband's murderer, and why Jane claimed to have seen the accident herself. Macaulay satirises the press, the pulpit, and fashionable thought in post-war London.
1221-a-preliminary-revision-of-the-north:
John M. Coulter revises the North American species of cactus, with Anhalonium and Lophophora, in a technical study for botanists. The work sorts species, describes forms, and sets out the marks that separate one from another. Coulter, a botanist at Chicago, revised cactus names that had grown tangled.

Coulter writes for specialists who need exact names and ranges, not for gardeners seeking colour. The revision remains a reference for cactus taxonomy, and a record of how the group was understood at the end of the nineteenth century. Anhalonium and Lophophora, desert plants of the Southwest, needed careful sorting.
12220-rada-a-drama-of-war-in-one-act:
Alfred Noyes, best known for narrative poems like The Highwayman, wrote Rada as a one-act war drama in 1913. The scene is a Balkan village just taken by the enemy, on Christmas Eve, in the guest chamber of a village doctor house.

Rada, the doctor wife, and her twelve-year-old daughter Subka face two hostile soldiers quartered in their home, Arram and Michael, while Nanko, a half-witted schoolmaster, capers by the fire. Looted goods appear, including a ring Subka swears is her father, and a gramophone meant as a Christmas gift. The play turns on what war does to a household: fear, defiance, and small kindnesses held against a night of occupation.
14055-food-guide-for-war-service-at-home:
Prepared in 1918 under the United States Food Administration with Herbert Hoover's preface, this guide taught teachers, pupils, and households how to eat for the war effort. Wheat, sugar, and fat had to stretch, since troops and allies needed supplies first. Simple statements of the food situation replace technical jargon, so a schoolroom could grasp why menus must change.

Victory bread anchors the rules. Bakers cut wheat with substitutes, first one-fifth and later one-quarter, and pies and cakes needed at least one-third substitute. Loaf sizes were fixed, prices watched, and fancy shapes banned. Sugar chapters praise corn syrup, molasses, honey, maple, and sorghum as stand-ins, with dried fruit for sweetness. Practical and patriotic, the guide turns kitchen choices into a form of service at home.
14558-darwinism-1889-an-exposition-of-th:
Alfred Russel Wallace, co-discoverer of natural selection, set out the theory in this 1889 exposition, in a second edition from Macmillan with portrait, map, and illustrations. Wallace wrote from Parkstone in Dorset.

Chapters define species, describe the struggle for existence among plants and animals, and weigh color, fertility, and variation as evidence. Wallace stresses selection's power while differing from Darwin on some points. The book is a clear, vigorous defense of Darwinism by its other father, and it remains a landmark of Victorian popular science. Wallace's fieldwork in the Malay Archipelago underpins his argument.
14602-war-brides-a-play-in-one-act:
Marion Craig Wentworth's one-act play War Brides, published by Century in 1915, protests war through women left behind. It was first produced at Keith's Palace Theatre in New York with Alla Nazimova as Hedwig. Photographs from the production illustrate the text.

Hedwig, pale and anxious, scorns the name war bride, showing a gold ring against Minna's iron one, while bugles and marching feet sound in the distance. Amelia, her mother, and soldiers' wives debate sacrifice and survival. The play is a short, passionate antiwar drama, famous in its day for Nazimova's performance.
15290-why-the-chimes-rang-a-play-in-one-:
Elizabeth Apthorp McFadden's one-act play Why the Chimes Rang, adapted from Raymond Alden's story, was published by Samuel French in 1915. A copyright notice warns that acting, public reading, or any use needs permission, with amateur royalties of five dollars per performance, paid a week ahead. Programs must credit the dramatization.

The play itself tells a Christmas tale of giving, in which chimes ring for a true gift. McFadden's stage version suits school and amateur groups. Readers who love Christmas drama will find the play short, sweet, and easy to stage.
1556-the-marriage-contract:
Balzac's novel of Bordeaux society follows Paul de Manerville, a young count who returns from Paris to marry Natalie Evangelista, a beautiful heiress. Around the marriage contract itself, lawyers, mothers, and friends bargain over dowries, settlements, and the future of two families, with every clause a move in a quiet war.

Paul learns too late that a marriage built on money and manners may starve the heart, and Natalie learns the price of a husband's pride. Balzac's eye for legal detail is at its sharpest here. The book is a cool, sad comedy of marriage as business in Restoration France.
16504-renaissance-in-italy-volumes-6-and:
John Addington Symonds closes his great Renaissance in Italy with this two-part study of the Catholic Reaction, issued in 1887. After five volumes on Italy's brilliant fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, he asks what stopped that growth. Spanish hegemony, the Sack of Rome in 1527, the siege of Florence, and the church's stern reply to reform all play a part.

Symonds writes with wide learning and a storyteller's sweep, moving from popes and princes to art, letters, and faith. The book forms the capstone of his life's work on Italy. Readers of cultural history will find it a grand, somber close to a golden age.
17111-the-meaning-of-the-war-life-matter:
Henri Bergson's short 1915 book, translated into English with an introduction by H. Wildon Carr, reads the Great War as a clash of life and matter. Bergson refuses the cool maxim of understand and do not condemn; he prefers anger that grows by grasping its object. A little history and philosophy, he says, will show the war's inner meaning.

He traces Germany from poetry, art, and thought to a new love of force and fact, and he sets life's creative push against matter's waste and drag. The second essay, on the force that wastes and the force that does not, extends the theme. Readers of wartime philosophy will find a brief, fiery defense of spirit against mechanism.
17269-weather-and-folk-lore-of-peterboro:
Charles Dack's 1911 Weather and Folk Lore of Peterborough and District continues his paper on surviving old customs, read at the Royal Archaeological Society in 1898. Peterborough sits where four counties nearly meet, so Dack gathers sayings from Huntingdon, Cambridge, Lincoln, and Northampton within about fifteen miles. Most were told to him in person, a few copied to complete the set.

May Day at Glatton fronts the book, with a John Clare motto on old customs loved however simple. The set suits folklore lovers and local historians tracing weather lore, customs, and country speech. Short and plain, it preserves a district's spoken wisdom before it faded from use.
17361-the-german-element-in-brazil-colon:
Benjamin Franklin Schappelle, a doctor of philosophy, published this study in Philadelphia in 1917. It is number twenty-six of Americana Germanica, a series on the literary, linguistic, and cultural relations of Germany and America. It opens with a song of the German Brazilians, then turns to the first settlers and to colonisation in the south of Brazil.

Schappelle traces how German colonies grew, how their speech changed far from home, and how colony life kept German ways alive in a new land. Readers get a scholarly but readable account of migration, language, and community. The book remains useful for the history of Germans abroad and for the study of dialects formed overseas.
1742-miss-civilization-a-comedy-in-one-a:
A society girl known as Miss Civilization walks into a hold-up one evening. The robbers behind the curtain find a young woman with more nerve than they have. Harry and Reddy, revolvers raised behind a curtain, expect an easy victim and meet a young woman whose nerve outmatches their own.

The play is short, bright, and built for performance, with its whole action turning on one reversal. Davis wrote it for the stage of his own day. It plays as a light satire: civilization, in the form of a well-bred girl, proves tougher than the outlaws who meant to rob it.
17621-one-day-more-a-play-in-one-act:
Joseph Conrad wrote this one-act play, issued by the Beaumont Press as its sixth book. The limited edition ran to twenty-four copies on Japanese vellum and two hundred and fifty on hand-made paper. This copy is number forty-six. The characters are Captain Hagberd, a retired coasting skipper, and Josiah Carvil, a blind widower and former shipbuilder. Harry Hagberd, the captain's son, ran away from home as a boy. A lamplighter and Bessie Carvil, Josiah's daughter, complete the cast.

The scene is a small seaport, and the play turns on waiting, return, and a father's long refusal to accept loss. Readers get Conrad in dramatic form, compressed and sombre, far from his novels' open seas. The play suits readers of Conrad and of early modern one-act drama.
17935-french-polishing-and-enamelling-a-:
Richard Bitmead wrote this practical manual on French polishing and enamelling, in a fourth edition printed in London in 1910. Bitmead had already written guides for cabinet-makers and upholsterers, and here he turns to the fine finish that gives wood its deep shine.

The book gives recipes for polishes, varnishes, glaze-lacquers, and revivers, with plain steps for each coat and rub. A worker learns how to fill grain, lay a smooth coat, and bring up a mirror gloss without streaks. It stays useful for restorers and wood workers, and it shows the craft pride of the old trade shops.
18905-the-war-and-unity-being-lectures-d:
The War and Unity gathers lectures given at the University of Cambridge Local Lectures Summer Meeting of 1918, edited by the Rev. D. H. S. Cranage and published by the University Press in 1919. Its governing idea is the power of Christianity to unite, tested first where Christians are grouped as Christians.

Lectures treat unity between denominations, with Stanton, Milner-White, Selbie, and Cooper on English, Scottish, and free churches. Further lectures cover unity between classes, by Bishop Woods and J. R. Clynes, unity in the empire, by F. J. Chamberlain, and unity between nations, by J. H. B. Masterman. The volume belongs to a wartime search for bonds stronger than division.
20443-the-letter-of-the-contract:
Basil King, the Canadian novelist, wrote The Letter of the Contract as a novel of home life and hard choices. Its heroine looks back on one small act that changed everything. Had she looked in on the children after her coffee, as she generally did, her whole life might have been different.

Instead she went down to the drawing room to write a note. From that tiny turn, the story builds its account of marriage, duty, and the terms people bind themselves by. King asks what we owe to the letter of our promises, and what we owe beyond it.
20787-punctuation-a-primer-of-informatio:
A man in a white hat and polished boots shows, without marks, how wild a sentence can run. Punctuation, a primer on the marks of punctuation, uses such tricks to teach its point. Commas, stops, and colons here get their due at last.

Frederick W. Hamilton wrote short primers that made dry craft clear and fun. This one sorts the marks by use, with crisp rules and bright cases. Writers, printers, and students all stood to gain from its order. The book proves a small point well made: clear marks save clear thought, on every page they touch.
21049-the-curlytops-and-their-pets-or-un:
Janet Martin loads her toy ship with oranges, gold, diamonds, and chocolate cake at the brook. Howard R. Garis opens The Curlytops and Their Pets on that rich, childish cargo. Teddy, her brother, sails boats beside her behind the house.

Ted and Janet, the Curlytops, collect pets and scrapes in this set of tales. Uncle Toby's strange collection of creatures gives this volume its hook. Garis, who created Uncle Wiggily, wrote shelves of warm animal tales for children. His Curlytops show the same gift: small wonders, kind hearts, and pets with minds of their own.
21537-expansion-and-conflict:
William E. Dodd, professor of American history at Chicago, wrote Expansion and Conflict, copyrighted in 1915. The book opens with Andrew Jackson defying the coalition that made John Quincy Adams president. Let the people rule, Jackson answered, as the party of the West rose.

Chapters move through Jackson's triumph, distress and reaction, and the militant South. War and conquest, the abolitionists, and a burst of prosperity follow. Stephen A. Douglas and Abraham Lincoln anchor the last third of the book. The appeal to arms and the collapse of the Confederacy close a swift survey of a nation splitting apart.
21643-the-kensington-district:
G. E. Mitton writes, and Sir Walter Besant edits, The Kensington District in the Fascination of London series. The booklet appeared in 1903, at one shilling and sixpence in cloth. Holland House, drawn by Herbert Railton, fronts the volume.

Besant's great survey aimed to record the whole of London, street by street. Kensington's palaces, gardens, and famed residents fill this part. The series also covered the Strand, Westminster, Chelsea, and Hampstead. Local folk and students of London both formed its target readers. Much of the city's interest, the editors held, lies in these street associations, and Kensington proves the point.
21785-poems-of-rural-life-in-the-dorset-:
Dorset farm life speaks in its own tongue in these poems by William Barnes, gathered here in one volume in 1903. Barnes wrote in the dialect of his home county, with its soft spellings and old words. A guide to the words and their sounds waits at the back of the book. His preface, written in June 1879, calls the poems glimpses of life and landscape in Dorset.

The verses move with the farming year: spring woods, Easter, milkmaids, great oak trees, and evening twilight. Barnes knew this world from inside and loved it without fuss. Thomas Hardy admired him, and later readers have too. The poems keep a whole way of rural English speech alive on the page.
22050-life-and-conduct:
J. Cameron Lees, a minister of the Church of Scotland, gathered his counsel in Life and Conduct, issued in 1896 for the Guild series. The book speaks chiefly to young men starting out. Lees lists the works he consulted and owns his debts openly. His aim is a plain guide to character that a busy reader can use.

Chapters treat habits, work, friendship, reading, and the formation of a steady mind. Lees mixes moral advice with literary illustration. The tone is earnest and Presbyterian, without gloom. Such conduct books filled the shelves of self-improving homes. Lees's volume is a fair, kindly example of the breed.
2502-chitra-a-play-in-one-act:
Rabindranath Tagore's Chitra, a play in one act, retells a Mahabharata story. Princess Chitra falls in love with Arjuna and asks the gods for a year of beauty to win him. The play follows her bargain, her love, and her final honesty, when she reveals her true self to the hero. Tagore's lyric prose gives the myth a tender, philosophical glow.

The drama's theme, that love must rest on truth rather than illusion, gives it lasting force. Tagore, the Nobel laureate, wrote it for a Western audience as well as an Indian one. Theater readers will find a beautiful short play.
2921-the-present-condition-of-organic-na:
Thomas Henry Huxley opened his 1863 lectures to working men with this survey of the present condition of organic nature. An editor's note presents Huxley, son of an Ealing schoolmaster, as a self-made intellectual. He passed through no regular course of education, yet shaped biology and scientific debate more than any other English scientist of his generation. The lecture sets out to state what is known before asking how it came to be.

Huxley traces a constant circulation between living and nonliving matter, as animals take in food, reject waste, die, and return their bodies to the inorganic world. That circulation frames the whole series on Darwin. The talk remains a clear introduction to ecology before the word existed, plain and confident.
3183-the-facts-concerning-the-recent-car:
Mark Twain opens this tale in high spirits, lighting a cigar as the morning mail arrives. The first letter bears a hand he loves: Aunt Mary's, the woman he honored most outside his own household. She had been his boyhood idol, and maturity, fatal to so many enchantments, had left his feeling for her intact. That warm start makes the turn that follows hit harder.

The carnival of the title is a parade of crimes, and the tale's engine is conscience itself, met in person and argued with face to face. Twain turns a moral idea into a comic fiend, then lets his narrator strike back. The story is short and savage about guilt: funny, uneasy, and unwilling to let its hero off clean.
3754-the-wonders-of-instinct-chapters-in:
Jean Henri Fabre, the French schoolteacher turned naturalist, records a lifetime of insect watching at his home in Serignan, the Harmas. His chapters follow the green grasshopper, the empusa, the burying beetles, and the pine processionary. The banded spider, the glow-worm, and the cabbage caterpillar each get patient notes on what the creature does and how it does it. Experiments form the core, as Fabre tests burial, hunting, and procession with simple traps and trials.

The prose stays close to the ground, with a dead mouse lashed to a bar or a ring of caterpillars breaking in the cold. Fabre argues from sight rather than theory, and his wonder never dulls. Readers curious about animal minds will find a classic of natural history, written by a man who watched one garden for decades and saw a world in it.
433-the-conflict:
David Graham Phillips follows Jane Hastings, a restless young woman home from Wellesley and Europe, in this novel. Jane, trained for a full life, finds her Indiana town offers her only marriage: to drop her name and vanish into a husband's life. She refuses that bargain and seeks work of her own.

Factories, railways, and town politics fill her view from the old house above Remsen City. Phillips tracks Jane's clash with kin, suitors, and custom as she claims a public role. The novel stands as a frank early portrait of a woman who wants a life, not merely a match.
5165-innocent-her-fancy-and-his-fact:
Marie Corelli's novel is told in two books, Her Fancy and His Fact, following a young woman named Innocent. The first book follows her romantic imagination along a rambling country road into a green dell. The second tests those dreams against a man's harder view of the world, as love, reputation, and choice collide.

Corelli contrasts a heroine's inner life with the facts that threaten it, in her usual lush and moralising style. The novel will appeal to readers of Victorian romance who enjoy a story built around innocence, idealism. The question remains whether fancy or fact should rule a life.
6631-the-sculpture-and-mural-decorations:
Stella Perry surveys the sculpture and mural art of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco, with official photographs by the Cardinell-Vincent Company. An introduction by A. Stirling Calder, the exposition's chief of sculpture, frames the survey, and the book is dedicated to the memory of Karl Bitter. A Keats sonnet on fears of dying before his work is done opens the mood.

Each work gets a picture and a plain description, so readers can tour the fair's art without leaving home. The volume, copyright 1915, captures a brief, grand moment in American public art. It suits lovers of sculpture, murals, and world's fair history alike.
7-the-mayflower-compact:
Passengers bound for Virginia found themselves off Cape Cod in November 1620. Their Mayflower Compact bound them into a civil body politic before landing. The signers promised to frame just laws for the general good of the colony.

The compact names God, King James, and the voyage's aims in its opening lines. It then pledges submission to laws and offices the settlers would create. Signed by the adult men aboard, it became a first model of self-government in New England. The short text still anchors American ideas of consent. The compact's plain prose still reads as a founding act of consent.
7261-the-siksha-patri-of-the-svami-naray:
The Shiksha Patri of the Svami Narayana sect appears here in Sanskrit text, edited by Professor Monier Williams for the Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society in 1882. Williams notes that the text was lithographed in Samvat 1928, or 1872, by order of the heads of the sect, with a Gujarati commentary. The file marks long vowels with circumflexes in place of macrons.

The sect, a modern Vaishnava movement, thus reaches English readers through a scholarly journal rather than through popular print. The short text carries rules and teaching for its followers, preserved with the care of a learned edition. This volume holds the Sanskrit text and its editorial framing.
7417-the-resources-of-quinola-a-comedy-i:
Honoré de Balzac, the great novelist, tried the stage with this comedy, first presented at the Odéon in Paris on March 19, 1842. A prologue and five acts follow Quinola, a resourceful schemer whose inventions and plans drive the comic plot. Balzac's preface defends the venture frankly: praise for his novels had been lavish, and a first play is harder than a first novel.

The comedy turns on ingenuity itself: a man of ideas seeking backing, recognition, and reward in a world that prefers safe reputations. Old notes in the volume even touch the history of invention, including claims about steam locomotion before the famous names. The play shows Balzac the dramatist, using the stage to test the same ambitions and illusions that fill his novels.
7450-terre-napoleo-n-a-history-of-french:
Ernest Scott's history takes its name from Terre Napoléon, the name French explorers gave to the southern coast of Australia. Its main object is the expedition Napoleon Bonaparte sent to Australia in 1800 to 1804, and the opinions long current about its purpose. Scott, who once accepted the leading authorities without doubt, re-examines the evidence with fresh eyes.

The plan sets the colonial rivalry of Britain and France first, then brings the French ships and the British discovery ship Investigator onto the same coasts at about the same time. Were the French after science, or after a colony? Scott weighs the documents, with eight illustrations and maps to guide the reader. The book is a model of careful revisionist history, second edition 1911.
7992-better-homes-in-america-plan-book-f:
This plan book served Demonstration Week, October 9 to 14, 1922, in the Better Homes in America campaign, launched by an advisory council and carried on by representative women across the country. It opens with a White House letter of July 21, 1922, in which President Harding endorses the campaign. Stressing not only home ownership as a foundation of citizenship but also furnishing, sanitation, and equipment. The campaign argued that the home deserved the same care given to factory conditions.

The book is a practical guide for local organisers: model homes, exhibits, and advice for building and furnishing a decent house. It captures a moment when America treated better housing as a public cause. For historians of domestic life, it shows what reformers counted as a good home, and how they tried to spread that standard town by town.
8142-the-riot-act:
The Riot Act, passed in 1714 and effective in August 1715, is printed here in full from the Statutes at Large, chapter five of the first year of George I. The transcriber notes that many sources date the act to 1715, but the statute book gives 1714, with the confusion arising from its effective date. The act provides for preventing tumults and riotous assemblies, and for the more speedy and effectual punishing of rioters.

This short statute gave English its famous phrase, read them the Riot Act, since magistrates had to read a proclamation before force could be used against a crowd. The text is brief and legalistic, but its influence on public order law was long. For readers of legal history, it is the original document behind a phrase still in everyday use.
9505-four-girls-and-a-compact:
Annie Hamilton Donnell wrote Four Girls and a Compact in 1908, a girls' tale of friendship and a grand plan. Four girls of a little colony they call the B-Hive gather for tea in kimonos and slippers. Loraine, the queeny-named leader, rules the group, while Laura Ann sighs at near misses. T.O., short and often late, arrives wet and cheerful to join the plot.

The compact binds the girls to some shared aim, tested by fun, quarrels, and growing pains. Donnell writes with light humor and warm feeling for girlhood bonds. A reader gets a cozy, old-style schoolgirl story, full of chatter, loyalty, and the joy of plans made together.
9829-the-jewel-merchants-a-comedy-in-one:
James Branch Cabell wrote this one-act comedy in New York in 1921, with a prologue spoken by the author himself. The play takes jewel merchants as its subject, and lets bargaining over precious stones stand in for bargaining over love, pride, and reputation.

Because it runs a single act, the comedy moves fast: sharp talk, quick reversals, and a neat ending. Cabell, known for his invented kingdom of Poictesme, here works in a smaller, modern key. It is a good short sample of his wit, and an easy first taste of his stage writing.
a-preliminary-revision-of-the-north-amer:
John Merle Coulter, a working botanist, sets out to bring order to the cacti of North America in this technical revision. His title names the ground: the species of Cactus, Anhalonium, and Lophophora found on the continent. The paper works through the plants name by name, sorting species that earlier writers had confused or split wrongly.

For each kind Coulter gives the marks that define it, its range, and its place in the family, using the dry, exact language of taxonomy. The study is not written for pleasure reading. It is a tool for herbaria and field botanists, and it laid groundwork that later cactus science built on.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-collect:
Adrian Fortescue's entry explains the collect, a short prayer said before the Epistle at Mass. It is repeated at Lauds, Terce, Sext, None, and Vespers. The Latin collecta matches the Greek synaxis, a gathering. The name first fit a station-day rite. People met at one church, prayed, then walked in procession to the station church. The celebrant's prayer opened the march. Innocent III later read the name another way, as the priest gathering up the prayers of all the people.

Only the first of three matching prayers still bears the name. The Secret and Post-Communion follow the same pattern. Fortescue sets out how collects are said and the celebrant's gestures at Dominus vobiscum. He covers the old rule of uneven numbers and the customs of standing or kneeling. Standing during collects, long neglected, was happily coming back.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-contract:
The entry sets out contract's canonical doctrine, developed from Roman civil law. In Roman law a mere agreement to give, do, or refrain formed a nude pact, giving no civil obligation and no action. It needed clothing in some fact the law recognized before an enforceable obligation arose. Canonical doctrine leaves hardly room for the nude pact versus contract distinction.

Four elements stand: consent, capacity, lawful subject-matter, and lawful consideration. Mutual consent forms the contract, real not feigned, manifested so each knows the other consents. Consent must be deliberate and free, since grave obligation cannot spring otherwise. Subject-matter must be definite, possible, and honest. Civil law defines contract as several persons' coincident will determining their legal relations. Roman kinds run real, verbal, literal, and consensual. Even extinguishing a right implies a contract not to reassert it, and constitutions protect state charters for private purposes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dogmatic-fact:
A dogmatic fact, in the wider sense, is any fact tied to a dogma on which applying the dogma turns. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry asks whether Pius the Tenth is truly pope, duly elected and owned by the whole Church. That question touches dogma, since every duly elected pope is held to succeed Peter. Likewise, whether a council was truly ecumenical touches dogma, since such councils bear infallibility.

So does the question whether canonized saints truly died in the odor of sanctity, since all who so die are saved. The entry argues that the faithful owe inward assent to the Church's rulings on such facts. It grounds that duty in the matching roles of teacher and taught, pastor and flock.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elect:
Elect is a theological word for one chosen as an object of mercy and set apart for eternal life, and this entry traces its use through the Bible. In the Old Testament the term falls chiefly on Israel as God's people, or on Israelites faithful to their call. Deuteronomy and the later Isaiah use it often, and the Psalms, Tobit, Wisdom, and Sirach apply it to God's true servants.

In the New Testament the title passes from Israel to the members of the Church, on earth and in heaven. Peter calls them a chosen generation and a kingly priesthood, called from darkness into light. Paul lists five steps in their election: foreknown, predestined, called, justified, and glorified. John gives the name to those who fight beside the Lamb, and Luke says God hears their cries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epact:
An epact is the surplus of the solar over the lunar year. More loosely, it is the age of the moon in days on 1 January. The system rests on the Metonic lunar cycle. It tells on which days of the year the moons fall. The calendar grew from the need to date Easter aright.

The Last Supper fell on the Jewish Passover, kept on the fourteenth day of the first month. That month began with the new moon whose fourteenth day fell on or after the spring equinox. Christ rose on Sunday, the seventeenth day of the paschal moon. An Easter anniversary is possible only when that seventeenth day is a Sunday. To end disagreement, Nicaea in 325 ordered the Western rule for the whole Church: Easter on the Sunday after the fourteenth day of the moon. The Church used the Metonic cycle until the Gregorian reform of 1582.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-instinct:
Purposeful action that is not guided by awareness of its end is the rough core of instinct, though the entry warns that no single definition wins general assent. Popular and scientific writers have stretched the word in so many ways that a tight formula proves impossible. The working idea covers a chain of acts in a living being fitted to an end, without the being knowing that end.

Drawing the line proves the hard part. Reflex acts are bodily processes running through a fixed nerve path, while intelligent acts rest on knowledge, and instinct sits uneasily between them. Our limited knowledge of the inner processes may leave a given act hard to place, the entry admits, but theory can still mark the borders clearly. Readers get a careful sorting of three kinds of action.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-intellect:
Thought itself, as the higher spiritual power of the soul to know, is the topic of this philosophy entry. Catholic usage reserves the words intellect, intelligence, and intellectual for that higher power, which sense wakes into action but which reaches beyond sense in range. Its acts include attention, forming concepts, judging, reasoning, reflection, and awareness of self.

Each of those acts shows an element beyond the senses, the entry argues. Together they reveal a knowing power of a higher order than mere sense perception requires. Many modern psychologists stretch the same words to cover sense-based knowing too, a usage the entry says breeds confusion. Readers get a clear statement of the older distinction and why its author thinks the narrower use should be kept.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-interdict:
A church penalty that bars persons, places, or acts from sacred things is the strict sense of interdict in this canon law entry. Roman law first used the word for a praetor's interim order, above all over possession, and both Roman and canon law keep that older sense. In looser speech a priest, a church, or a devotion can be called interdicted. That happens when the priest is suspended, the building secularized or closed, or a practice halted.

Strictly, though, interdict applies to persons and places under a formal ban, and the entry works through its kinds, effects, and lifting. A church may fall under it because the building has suffered pollution or lost its consecration, so that divine service must stop for a time. Readers get a precise legal term rescued from its everyday looseness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-medal-of-sain:
The Medal of Saint Benedict, once a cross, serves devotion to him. One face shows the saint bearing a cross and the Holy Rule. Beside the image stand a cup and a raven, under the words Crux Sancti Patris Benedicti, Cross of the Holy Father Benedict. Around the rim runs a plea for guard at death by his presence.

The reverse bears a cross whose bars carry initials for two Latin prayers. One reads Crux Sacra Sit Mihi Lux, the Holy Cross be my light. The other reads Non Draco Sit Mihi Dux, let not the dragon be my guide. Its angles repeat that cross. The rim gives the distich Vade Retro Satana, begone Satan, do not lure me with vanities. At the top stands Pax, peace, or the monogram IHS. The jubilee medal of 1880, for Benedict's fourteenth centenary, is struck only by Monte Cassino.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rule-of-st-be:
The Rule of St Benedict holds first place among monastic codes and was the most important factor in spreading western monasticism. Its exact time and place are unknown, nor can we tell whether it was composed whole or gradually. About 530 is a likely date, and Monte Cassino more probable than Subiaco, since the Rule shows Benedict's ripe monastic and spiritual insight.

The earliest chronicler says Monte Cassino's destruction by the Lombards in 581 sent the monks fleeing to Rome. They carried a copy of the Rule. By the mid-eighth century the pope's library held a copy believed to be Benedict's autograph. Pope Zachary presented this manuscript to Monte Cassino, and Charlemagne had a careful transcript made for his empire's monasteries. Several copies were made from it, one surviving today as Codex 914 of the St Gall Library.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-social-co:
Rousseau's Du Contrat Social, or Principles of Political Right, published in 1762, is the work analysed here. It survives as a fragment of a larger treatise on political institutions conceived during Rousseau's Venetian stay about 1741. Four books organise it, the first treating the formation of societies and the social contract itself.

Social order stands as a sacred right at the base of all other rights, and it does not come from nature. Family, most ancient and natural of societies, holds only by convention once children can fend for themselves. Slavery by nature confuses cause with effect, and force alone cannot ground right, since the strongest cannot stay strongest forever. Sovereignty, law, and government follow.
chitra-a-play-in-one-act:
Rabindranath Tagore drew his one-act play Chitra from the Mahabharata, and this English version appeared with Macmillan in 1914. His preface tells the source story. Arjuna, wandering in penance, meets Chitrangada, king's daughter of Manipur. She was raised as a son and heir, because her father's line was promised only one child per generation. Arjuna asks for her hand, and the king sets his condition about her future son.

Tagore reshapes the tale into lyrical drama. Chitrangada, scorned as unwomanly, wins a year of perfect beauty from the gods, captures Arjuna with it, and then must choose between the borrowed charm and her true self. The play asks whether love wants the mask or the person, in verse of great simplicity.

govdocs-archive_org-NrcReportOnPossibleL: A report of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission examines the possible long-term health effects of short-term exposure to radiation. Federal science reports of this kind weigh animal studies, accident data, and dose records to judge what a brief exposure may do over a lifetime. The question matters for workers and for communities near accidents and tests. Beyond its subject and maker, the archive record gives little detail of findings or date. It is held as a government technical report for readers of radiation health science.
govdocs-archive_org-cksonKingsDethroned1:
Kings Dethroned, published in 1922, was a sweeping attack on the authorities of modern science, and this extract holds its chapter 'Relativity Debunked.' The chapter takes on Albert Einstein's theory of relativity, then newly famous and still fighting for acceptance.

It covers the theory's reception at the Royal Astronomical Society in 1919, when eclipse observation results were announced as proof of Einstein. The author treats that moment as a coronation to undo, arguing the evidence had been oversold. The extract is early anti-relativity literature, held without endorsement as a record of the resistance Einstein faced.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-OtmoorProductio: A contents page survives from a manuscript about the investigation of James Earl Ray. Among its listed parts are a New Orleans trip and the Provincial Motel, a stop in Ray's travels that investigators retraced. The author is not identified. A contents page shows a book's architecture without its arguments: chapters planned, episodes chosen, order set. This one maps a Ray manuscript that may never have been published.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern:
In May 2016, a federal court in Buenos Aires found eighteen Argentine military officers guilty for their part in Operation Condor, the cross-border system of repression run by South America's military regimes. The National Security Archive's electronic briefing book, edited by Carlos Osorio and Peter Kornbluh, marked the verdict the day it landed.

Condor let member regimes seize, torture, and kill each other's dissidents far from home, and victims came from several countries. A trial that treated that system itself as the crime was a first in the region. The Archive hailed the ruling as a major milestone. Readers get both the outcome and the context: how a secret pact among dictatorships ended, forty years on, in open court.
innocent-her-fancy-and-his-fact:
Marie Corelli's Innocent: Her Fancy and His Fact begins with a reprobate of a road. The old by-road wanders down into a green, shadowy dell, past elder and hazel, to a farmyard gate. Book one, Her Fancy, belongs to the farm girl called Innocent. She dreams over books in a world of primroses and ploughed fields.

Innocent writes a novel in secret and sends it into the world. Its success carries her to London and to Hugo Jocelyn, the famous author she worships from afar. His Fact, the book's second half, measures the man against her fancy. Corelli, herself a best-selling author, pours her scorn for literary London into the tale. Innocence, genius, and betrayal make her plot. The by-road of the opening leads, as her roads do, to a moral reckoning.
lessons-in-music-form-a-manual-of-analys:
Percy Goetschius wrote Lessons in Music Form as a manual of analysis. Its subtitle promises all the structural factors used in musical composition. Oliver Ditson published it in Boston for a dollar and a half.

Goetschius held a royal professorship in Württemberg. He had written many theory books before this one. Here he teaches how pieces are built, section by section. Students learn to hear phrases, periods, and larger designs. The manual suits composers, teachers, and serious listeners alike. Examples from real composers anchor each design he names. Goetschius insists form is heard, not merely diagrammed.
miss-civilization-a-comedy-in-one-act:
Richard Harding Davis wrote this one-act comedy, first printed in Collier's Weekly. He founded it on a story by James Harvey Smith. The scene is a dining room on Long Island at Christmas. Silver presents still sit in red flannel bags on the sideboard.

The house belongs to railroad president James K. Gardner. His daughter Alice faces three uninvited guests. Their aliases are Gentleman Joe, Reddy the Kid, and Grand Stand Harry. A police captain completes the cast. Davis builds a light comedy of burglary and manners, where the young lady proves more than a match for her visitors.
nasa-tm-19670008871-excitation-of-hydrog:
S. P. Khare, working at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland as a resident research associate, studies a basic atomic collision in this paper. It is the third part of his series on exciting the hydrogen molecule by electron impact. This part treats singlet-triplet excitations, collisions in which an incoming electron flips the molecule into a spin state that light alone cannot reach.

Khare used one-center wave functions developed by Huzinaga, together with the Ochkur approximation, to compute the exchange excitation. Because the lowest triplet state pushes the molecule's two atoms apart, these excitations split hydrogen molecules into separate atoms. The shape of his predicted curve for that splitting matched the lab data of Corrigan in general. He also computed rates for the splitting and for related continuous radiation, and compared them with the measurements at hand.
nasa-tm-19690018501-possible-initial-evi:
F. W. Stecker, of the Theoretical Studies Branch at Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this preprint, X-641-69-232. He presented it at an astronomy symposium in Rome in May 1969. Stecker compares recent cosmic background gamma ray observations against spectra predicted by several cosmic interactions. He argues the best match points beyond our own galaxy.

The even, all-sky gamma glow is best explained, he finds, by decaying particles born in extragalactic cosmic ray collisions. That reading implies such sources were more active in the distant past. They began forming only tens of millions of years after the big bang, on his estimate. Today's extragalactic cosmic ray flow is inferred as a tiny fraction of the galactic one.
nasa-tm-19690021377-primary-chemical-met:
Aaron Fisher, John Grimsley, Thomas Sciacca, and Charles Staugaitis, of Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this June 1969 report, X-735-69-230. They catalog the primary techniques for evaluating magnetic tapes: chemical, metallurgical, and electro-optical. Tapes then recorded much of NASA's spacecraft and test data, so judging tape quality before use protected whole archives.

The chemical section runs from light spectrum tests to heat-based breakdown tools and thermal analyzers. Each tool reads a different trait of the tape's binder and oxide coating. Metal and machine procedures follow: cross-section making, close-up views, and head-tape fit checks. Blocking, tensile, hardness, and surface roughness tests complete the practical kit the authors assembled.
nasa-tm-19700021514-description-and-perf:
Pierre A. Thollot, Richard C. Bainbridge, and James Nestor of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 energy conversion conference in Las Vegas. It describes the electrical subsystem of a Brayton power system. The system size ranges from two to fifteen kilowatts of electric power.

The subsystem covers the alternator and the gear that conditions its output. Liquid coolant runs through a heat exchanger and the alternator housing to carry heat away. The paper gives both the design and how the hardware performed in tests. Power systems of this class were leading candidates for long missions in deep space.
nasa-tm-19700025308-a-preliminary-analys:
Clarke T. Hackler of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston prepared this internal note, number 66-M-32. It gives a first analysis of failure detection during the lunar module's powered descent. It also covers how the guidance system would be watched for faults during that flight phase, the most demanding minutes of the mission.

During descent the guidance flies the craft almost the whole way down, while the crew only monitors. Hackler notes that comparing the primary and abort guidance paths builds confidence that both work. Spotting that one has failed, though, is easier than proving which one failed. His study takes up that gap: watching both systems, detecting a failure, and isolating it while a safe abort is still possible.
nasa-tm-19710011034-a-summary-of-major-n:
Kennedy Space Center issued this reference as Historical Report Number 1, revised in 1970. It sums up major NASA launchings from October 1, 1958 through September 30, 1970. Those dates span the agency's first twelve years. The summary covers flights from the Eastern Test Range and the Western Test Range.

The Historical and Library Services Section at Kennedy compiled the record. Readers get a compact account of the launch campaigns that built the early space program. It captures the shift from small test rockets to crewed Apollo flights. Historians still use such summaries to check dates, vehicles, and launch sites.
nasa-tm-19710011291-experimental-investi:
James E Calogeras, Charles M Mehalic, and Paul L Burstadt of the Lewis Research Center ran this turbojet distortion study. Screens placed before a J85 engine warped the incoming air pressure on purpose. The team measured how each warp pattern cut the engine stall margin, the safety gap before the compressor stalls.

One clear result stood out. The compressor had a critical distortion angle of sixty degrees. Stall losses for single and multiple patterns tracked a simple index based on the lowest mean pressure in any sixty degree sector. Hub radial distortion changed pumping and pressure but not stall margin. Tip radial distortion did change stall margin.
nasa-tm-19710011753-a-study-of-the-requi:
R W Jech of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for an April 1971 meeting on composite materials in Anaheim. It asks how long reinforcing fibers must be inside a composite to do their job. The test material paired tungsten wire fibers with a copper matrix. Length relative to width is called the aspect ratio.

Jech compared pull out specimens in tension and in stress rupture tests. The critical aspect ratio in hot stress rupture tests ran slightly above the tension value. Above that ratio, the tungsten fiber controlled how long specimens lasted. Below it, the copper matrix controlled failure time. The results guide fiber length choices for parts under long hot loads.
nasa-tm-19720013138-the-recurrent-nature:
A NASA preprint on solar radio noise studies type 1 noise active regions from 1965 through 1969. Its author was a NASA associate with the University of Maryland. Type 1 noise comes from active regions on the Sun at meter wavelengths. Because the Sun rotates, a long-lived region returns to view roughly every twenty-seven days.

The study tracks that recurrence across five years of observations. The abstract reports a repeat period slightly longer than twenty-seven days for these noise sources. It also finds that the number of recurrent trends for a source is generally four. Discussion connects the noise sources closely with the active regions where proton flares occur. Earlier work by Sakurai and Stone on the 1968 season had found the same near twenty-seven-day rhythm.
nasa-tm-19720022222-predictions-of-vehic:
A NASA radiation forecast predicts the electron and proton fluxes the UK-4 spacecraft would meet in orbit. UK-4 was a British satellite built with NASA cooperation, and the scan garbles the forecast's author names. Designers needed to know how much particle radiation UK-4 would meet in orbit. Its planned path crossed Earth's radiation belts twice on every revolution.

To make the predictions, the authors added up proton and electron flows along the planned flight path. Current models of Earth's field and of the radiation environment fed those sums. Because the launch was set for late 1971, close after a solar maximum, the electron data needed two adjustments. Artificial electrons left by the 1962 Starfish explosion had to be decayed away to natural background levels. Lasting solar-cycle effects in the outer belt, missing from the older environment model, also had to be folded in.
one-day-more-a-play-in-one-act:
Joseph Conrad wrote this one-act play for the stage. The Beaumont Press issued it as its sixth book. Only 274 numbered copies were printed in this edition. Captain Hagberd is a retired coasting skipper in the cast. His son Harry ran away from home as a boy.

Josiah Carvil is a blind, widowed former shipbuilder. His daughter Bessie, about twenty-five, guides him patiently. The scene is a small sea port at dusk. Two yellow brick cottages stand by a lamp post. Carvil scolds Bessie for hurrying his steps homeward. Conrad builds quiet tension from waiting and return.
potterism-a-tragi-farcical-tract:
Rose Macaulay published Potterism in 1920, subtitling it a tragi-farcical tract, and dedicated it to the unsentimental precisians in thought. Who have no fit habitation on this confused, inaccurate, and emotional planet. Potterism, her coinage, names the mental disease of the age: cant, sentimentality, and loose thinking. Spread by the press empire of the Potter family, whose newspapers teach millions to feel instead of think. Epigraphs from Johnson, Bacon, and Evelyn Underhill arm the attack.

Macaulay, just back from war work, wrote the satire as a novel of ideas. Following the Potter children and their circle as the family gospel of mush conquers English life, with tragedy leaking through the farce. Her target is not feeling but fake feeling, language smeared until truth cannot be seen. A century on, readers will recognize every symptom; Macaulay simply named the condition first and funniest.
rada-a-drama-of-war-in-one-act:
Rada, a drama of war in one act by Alfred Noyes, is dated 1913. It is set in the Balkans, in a village just taken by the enemy, on Christmas Eve. Rada, wife of the village doctor, must house two hostile soldiers, Arram and Michael. Her daughter Subka, aged twelve, shares the room. So does Nanko, a half-witted schoolmaster.

The scene is the doctor's guest-chamber, lit by fire, candles, and the lamp that burns always before the icon screen with its three gilded icons. Rada sits weeping on the divan with her head in her hands while the two soldiers drink at the table, and the idiot chuckles by the fire.
renaissance-in-italy-volumes-6-and-7-of-:
John Addington Symonds closed his Renaissance in Italy with The Catholic Reaction, in two parts, issued by Henry Holt of New York in 1887. Verses from Savonarola stand at the front. His preface calls the study a needed supplement to the five former volumes, closing the epoch they opened.

His subject is the Catholic Revival, by nature reactionary, and the causes that halted Italy's growth along Renaissance lines. Symonds analyzes Spain's position in the peninsula, the conduct of the Council of Trent, and the working of the Holy Office and the Company of Jesus. He also weighs the state of the society on which those forces bore.
terre-napoleo-n-a-history-of-french-expl:
Ernest Scott wrote Terre Napoleon, a history of French probes and plans in Australia, first printed on July 7, 1910, with a second printing in 1911 from Methuen of London. Eight plates and maps support the text.

Scott says his aim is to set out the facts of the voyage Napoleon sent to Australia from 1800 to 1804. That voyage, led by Captain Nicolas Baudin, charted shores that French maps marked Terre Napoleon. Scott once took the standard views of its aim on trust, then found them shaky when he checked the facts. Readers get a close test of claims that France meant to seize land in the south, drawn from logs and maps.
the-conflict:
David Graham Phillips wrote The Conflict, a novel that opens on Jane Hastings, home again after four years at Wellesley and two more split among Paris, Dresden, and Florence. She looks down from her family's big house on the lawns and gardens above Remsen City, a factory town in south central Indiana cut through by rail lines.

Jane has trained for an active life and finds nothing ahead but marriage, which she fears would erase her name and self. She has met no man she would give herself up for, and she insists there must be work for her beyond wifehood. Then a young man in a cap and knickerbockers climbs the road toward the house, and her grave mood gives way to charm.
the-facts-concerning-the-recent-carnival:
Mark Twain tells this tale in the first person, starting on a glad morning when a letter comes from his Aunt Mary. She is the one person whose pleas could once stir his conscience about smoking, though even her power has now faded.

Just as the narrator feels ready to forgive any foe, the door opens. In walks a shriveled dwarf, barely two feet high, bent and odd in every part, with sharp fox-like eyes full of cunning and spite. Twain builds the comic horror slowly: the small guest is the narrator's own conscience, come to settle accounts for a life of small sins.
the-german-element-in-brazil-colonies-an: Benjamin Franklin Schappelle wrote The German Element in Brazil, a study of colonies and dialect printed at Philadelphia in 1917 as number twenty-six of Americana Germanica. Only the front matter is present here: the series page, a dedication to Joseph G. Rosengarten, and the head of the contents, which starts with a song of the German Brazilians. No chapter text can be read in what is present, so the study's findings cannot be described from the front matter alone.
the-jewel-merchants-a-comedy-in-one-act:
James Branch Cabell published this one-act comedy in New York in 1921. He dedicated it to Louise Burleigh. She was, he says, the first source of its notions. His prologue concedes the play's limits at once. It has no claim to fine writing, he admits. It was made for the little theatre stage. Its one clear virtue is that it acts easily. It plays rather well, he adds.

Candor compels the rest of the tale. The Little Theatre League of Richmond bullied him into the work. They wanted his story Balthazar's Daughter on stage. His first draft read well but would not act. Its speech was unspeakable, he says. Rehearsals under Burleigh changed a line here and more there. Each rehearsal produced a different play. The prologue shows how a cast rewrites its author.
the-marriage-contract:
Honoré de Balzac's The Marriage Contract, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley and dedicated to Rossini, opens with a father's history. Monsieur de Manerville was a Norman gentleman who married one of the richest heiresses of Bordeaux and became a Gascon for her château de Lanstrac. In 1790 he sailed to Martinique, leaving his property with an honest notary's clerk named Mathias, and so escaped the Revolution's dangers; he returned to find his possessions intact and well managed.

His wife died in 1810, and the old man, having learned the value of worldly goods in a dissipated youth, grew miserly. His only son Paul came home from the college of Vendôme that year to three years of close paternal discipline. The tyranny of a man of seventy, Balzac says, cost Paul the faculty of resistance that begets moral courage, preparing the son's part in the contract to come.
the-mayflower-compact:
The Mayflower Compact is the short agreement signed at Cape Cod on November 11, 1620, by the men of the Mayflower. Its signers call themselves loyal subjects of King James and state their purpose plainly. They had undertaken a voyage to plant the first colony in the northern parts of Virginia. Their stated ends were the glory of God, the advancement of the Christian faith, and the honor of king and country.

In the document the signers covenant and combine themselves into a civil body politic. They promise to enact just and equal laws, ordinances, and offices for the general good of the colony. Every signer pledges due submission and obedience to what the body frames. The list of names includes John Carver, William Bradford, Edward Winslow, William Brewster, Miles Standish, and John Alden. Readers get, in a few lines, the founding act of self-government at Plymouth.
the-meaning-of-the-war-life-matter-in-co:
Henri Bergson's The Meaning of the War, subtitled Life and Matter in Conflict, reached English readers in June 1915 through T. Fisher Unwin of London. H. Wildon Carr supplied the introduction, dated May 1915. The contents list two addresses: Life and Matter at War, and The Force Which Wastes and That Which Does Not Waste. Demand was quick enough that second and third impressions followed within three months.

Bergson opens by refusing a famous maxim that philosophy ends in understanding without indignation. Faced with crime, he says, he would rather give his indignation rein than merely understand. Happily, he adds, the choice need not be made, since some forms of anger sharpen thought instead of blinding it. Written while the First World War raged, the addresses cast the conflict as a struggle between life and brute matter. Readers get a great philosopher speaking as a French citizen in wartime.
the-present-condition-of-organic-nature-:
Thomas H. Huxley's lecture The Present Condition of Organic Nature was the first of six lectures to working men, given at the Museum of Practical Geology in 1863. Its subject is Darwin's Origin of Species. An editor's note introduces Huxley as the most noteworthy English thinker of his century in science. The note stresses that he was a self-made intellectual. His schooling was two chaotic years in a pandemonium of a school, with no help after that until manhood.

The note follows him from geology reading at twelve to a medical degree and a gold medal. A navy surgeon post took him aboard the Rattlesnake for survey work in Torres Straits. Tropical sea life drew him, and studying it began his great career. His dates are given: born at Ealing in 1825, dead at Eastbourne in 1895. A publisher's notice explains how shorthand notes of the lectures came to be printed.
the-resources-of-quinola-a-comedy-in-a-p:
Honore de Balzac defends his comedy in a preface written after its first performance at the Theatre de l'Odeon in Paris on March 19, 1842. He admits that a first venture on stage is harder than success in prose, however praised his romances have been.

Balzac predicts critics will one day use this play as a battering ram against newer plays, just as they used his novels against Quinola itself. He also protests that nearly fifty reviewers dismissed as invented the historic fact, tied to the history of steam, on which the play rests. Playwright and novelist meet uneasily in this apologia.
the-riot-act:
Jonathan Walther transcribed the full statute in February 2002. His source was a 1764 printing of the Statutes at Large. Many sources date the act to 1715, he notes. The statute book itself says 1714 instead. The act took effect in August of 1715. It aims at preventing tumults and riotous assemblies. It punishes rioters more swiftly and more surely.

Its preamble complains of rebellious riots across the kingdom. Public peace suffers under the tumults, it says. The king's person and government stand endangered by them. Existing punishments seem inadequate to such offences. Traduced ministers complete the preamble's grievances against the rioters. Readers meet the original law behind a famous phrase. Reading the Riot Act still means a stern warning today.
the-sculpture-and-mural-decorations-of-t: Stella G. S. Perry described The Sculpture and Mural Decorations of the Exposition, a pictorial survey of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition's art. Paul Elder and Company of San Francisco copyrighted it in 1915. The volume is dedicated to the memory of Karl Bitter. A sonnet by Keats follows the dedication. Only title matter, the dedication, the sonnet, and the start of the contents are present here. Perry's survey itself does not appear.
the-siksha-patri-of-the-svami-narayana-s:
Professor Monier Williams edited the Sanskrit text of the Sikshâ-Patrî of the Svâmi-Nârâyana sect for the Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society. The article appeared in the journal's new series, volume fourteen, published at London by Trübner and Company in 1882. Williams also supplied a translation of the text. His editorial note explains his sources. The text was lithographed in 1872 by order of the sect's heads, he says.

That lithographed version had a Gujarâtî commentary by Nityânanda-muni. The Wartâl Mahârâja gave Williams his copy on a first visit in 1875. It was full of mistakes, Williams found. He therefore followed a far more accurate manuscript instead. Its Sanskrit commentary was written by Pandit Satânanda-muni, a disciple of Svâmi-Nârâyana. For his translation Williams also studied that commentary, called Artha-dîpikâ, closely.
the-war-and-unity-being-lectures-deliver: The War and Unity collects lectures delivered at the Cambridge University local lectures summer meeting of 1918. D. H. S. Cranage of King's College edited the volume, published by Cambridge University Press in 1919. The pages present here give the imprint and the start of a contents list, so the lectures themselves do not appear. A first section treats unity between Christian denominations. Its opening lecture, A General View, is by V. H. Stanton, Regius Professor of Divinity, beginning at page one. A second lecture is titled The Church in the Furnace.
the-wonders-of-instinct-chapters-in-the-: J. H. Fabre's The Wonders of Instinct is represented here by its contents and a translators' note. Fourteen chapters study insects, from the green grasshopper to the glow-worm. Burying-beetles get two chapters, one on burial and one on experiments. Spiders, wasps, and the cabbage-caterpillar also appear. Bernard Miall translated two chapters, and Alexander Teixeira de Mattos translated the rest. The chapter texts do not follow in the pages present.
un-un-res-united-nations-participation-a:
American membership in the new United Nations was put into law by the United Nations Participation Act of 1945. Congress passed it months after the UN Charter was signed in San Francisco. The act gave the president the legal tools to seat the United States inside the world body from its first days.

The text covers the American ambassador's post, payment of dues, and the president's powers on the Security Council. It also sets limits on when American forces can serve under UN command. The act still stands, much amended, as the base law of the American role at the UN.
war-brides-a-play-in-one-act: Marion Craig Wentworth wrote War Brides, a play in one act. The Century Company issued it at New York in 1915, with photographs from the staging by Madame Nazimova. Wentworth dedicated it to her little boy Brandon. Pages present here hold the title pages and a list of pictures only, so the play itself is not shown. Captions name Hedwig, Amelia, Franz, and Arno. One caption shows a cry of good-by at the frontispiece. The title alone states the theme: women married in haste as the men march off.
weather-and-folk-lore-of-peterborough-an:
Charles Dack gathered the Weather and Folk Lore of Peterborough and District for the Peterborough Natural History, Scientific, and Archaeological Society in 1911. Charles Hawkins printed it in King Street. A motto from John Clare praises old customs, however simple, as welcome and dear. The pages here open a second series. It continues a paper on the survival of old customs, read before an archaeological society in 1898. More customs are added, with fuller word on others.

Dack explains a local puzzle at the start. Peterborough stands where four counties almost meet within a stone's throw. Its sayings thus carry the traditions of Huntingdon, Cambridge, and Lincoln, as well as Northampton. Pinning one saying to one county is hard, so he prints the sayings as he finds them. A drawing of May Day at Glatton in 1856, by the Rev. E. Bradley, fronts the book.
why-the-chimes-rang-a-play-in-one-act: The front pages here hold copyright and royalty terms for Why the Chimes Rang, a one-act play by Elizabeth Apthorp McFadden, while the play itself does not appear. Samuel French published it in New York and London, copyrighted in 1915. McFadden adapted Raymond McDonald Alden's story of the same name. Amateur groups could stage it for five dollars a performance, paid a week ahead. All programs had to note the source story and its publisher, Bobbs-Merrill. Professional rates were given on request.
